prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought frequency metrology to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean invention with an unusually crisp attribution: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift, and Ye's group carried the performance to the systematic frontier and into many-body clock physics. It has been reproduced independently in several species and laboratories, clocks are compared across continents, and it underpins the discussion of a redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy. It is a measurement-limited, instrument-driven advance of the kind I value as an experimentalist, and it drew the broadest opening support (eight of eight ballots, three first places, six top-three). Having ranked it second myself, I now think it is the strongest configuration the committee can defend on both merit and attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that it follows the 2005 prize on frequency-comb technology and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems, so a sceptic can call it incremental on recognised metrology. The credit may also understate other strontium and ytterbium groups (for example in Paris, Boulder and PTB) who made key demonstrations, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. In my own view the best alternative is IceCube (B052), which I ranked first. It opens a new observational window, but the source identification is still at moderate significance and the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the precursor projects is harder to settle, so I do not insist on it this year.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first as a clean founding invention (Katori's magic wavelength) realised at record performance by Ye, reproduced in many national laboratories and showing no sign of premature recognition.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll on the attribution and on maturity, and this is where the case is strongest. I would add a qualification he only touches on: because Sr and Yb groups elsewhere made important demonstrations, the citation should be framed around the invention and its realisation at the 10^-18 level rather than around who was first to a particular number. I also think his second choice, atom interferometry (B001), is weaker, since its fundamental-physics payoff is still maturing and Chu's earlier prize complicates the credited trio.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B052) first as a discovery of a new window on the universe, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the credited leaders, while acknowledging that the three-name split simplifies a large collaboration and ignores the precursor projects.
responses.response: I share his scientific judgement, since I ranked B052 first myself, but I differ on attribution. I would credit only Halzen and Karle, and adding Spiering without Baikal, DUMAND or AMANDA contributors makes the allocation look arbitrary. Only Danielsson and I placed B052 first and Olsson put it seventh, so opening support is thin. The source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still at moderate significance, so waiting costs the prize little. I now keep B052 as the principal alternative and not as my proposal.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B009 and ranks the optical-lattice quantum simulation theme (B010) second, noting that four credited names cannot fit into three and that Esslinger is the arguable omission, with Zoller's credit overlapping other candidates.
responses.response: I agree that B010 has the attribution problem he describes: Zoller's proposal work, Greiner and Bloch's Mott-insulator realisation and Esslinger's fermion experiments are separable and one of them must be left out, and Zoller's credit also overlaps B014. That makes B010 harder to fund as a single clean part than the clock. I would also resist treating a high Borda score for B010 as proof of its merit, since it is split across theory and several experimental groups. I therefore do not put it among my two alternatives.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B009 first, stressing that the clock transitions rest on careful relativistic many-body atomic structure, and ranks the topological insulator candidate (B018) second.
responses.response: I accept her point that the atomic-structure input is part of why the clocks reach 10^-18, and it strengthens my view that the physics is substantial and not only technical. On B018 I hold a qualification: she and I both note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect, and that the 3D materials work is also not credited, so the three-name configuration leaves out significant people. I keep B018 as a second alternative because its maturity and conceptual weight are high, but my preference is for the clock.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B017) first as a clearly defined invention with Rose, Haider and Urban as a natural triple, mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: The invention is real and the credit is tidy, and I take seriously her argument that a prize for an instrument is entirely consistent with the 'discovery or invention' criterion, which I apply to IceCube myself. I still think that B017 enables a great deal of materials science but does not itself deliver a new physical measurement of comparable reach, whereas the clock enables new tests of fundamental physics. Krivanek's competing claim on STEM aberration correction also needs to be settled. Only Olsson ranked B017 high, with Eriksson eighth, so I do not see support for it as the principal choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to wait for stronger source-identification evidence before recognising IceCube, and how to settle credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors.
How much the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems should discount optical lattice clocks as a further metrology award.
Whether a redefinition of the second, expected but not yet decided, should be awaited before the award.
I rely on my background knowledge of the results and cannot independently verify internal credit within collaborations.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B009, since my documented connections are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, none of which are clocks. For B052 I note a field proximity: I am an astroparticle experimentalist at KTH who may be perceived as favouring a neighbouring detector-driven discovery, although my profile records no IceCube membership or personal tie to the credited names, so I am not recommending recusal.
